issues.legal_issue: An order of a civil court acting as the appellate authority under the eviction statute is not amenable to a writ of certiorari under Article 226 of the Constitution.

The High Court may exercise Article 227 supervisory jurisdiction over a civil court’s order only on limited grounds and may not use it as an appellate jurisdiction to correct a merely erroneous decision.

The High Court exceeded its writ and supervisory jurisdiction by framing points for determination in pending summary eviction proceedings, thereby substituting its judgment for that of the statutory authority.
The prior final determination of the status of the premises and the occupants’ rights barred those matters from being reopened under the doctrine of res judicata.
The Limitation Act’s provisions governing suits, appeals and applications before judicial fora do not apply to eviction proceedings before an Inquiry Officer that are administrative in character.
Whether occupants may claim a right to remain in possession under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is a matter for the Inquiry Officer to determine if raised.
An Inquiry Officer’s employment by the public authority does not, without personal interest or bias, invalidate eviction proceedings on grounds of institutional bias.
The State Government is not a necessary party to eviction proceedings concerning premises belonging to the public authority.
Eviction proceedings may continue in the absence of regulations under section 105H if the Inquiry Officer follows the principles of natural justice.
